Note that theme-3's R14 already got this right by gating its inventory watermark on 'AND the plan band is NORMAL'; R-09 must inherit the same guard. Without it the two recommendations produce a tick that loops without a legal action.

reviews.reasoning: The pacing bands are the right shape and are the single most valuable proposal across all three themes. But band (b) — 'THROTTLE: N_MAX=1 and routine tier only, no new hard-tier launches' — is a direct, unresolved collision with the operator's PRIMARY priority. Tier selects model, effort AND lens-battery depth (per DOCT-06 and R-17), so forcing routine tier under credit pressure ships security- and netcode-surface work with a thinner review gauntlet precisely when the loop is least able to afford rework. The recommendation's own risk note half-acknowledges this and then proposes an exemption only for 'security/RLS/schema surfaces'.
reviews.correction: Resolve the tradeoff explicitly rather than exempting a list: under credit pressure the correct move is to launch FEWER slices at full tier, never the same number at reduced tier. Band (b) should reduce N_MAX and defer hard-tier slices to the next plan week — it must not demote them. A demoted hard slice that produces a residual costs two slices' credits for one slice of capability, which is a net LOSS against the value-per-credit objective, whereas deferring costs nothing (idle hours are free per operator correction A).

reviews.reasoning: The experiment design is sound and the confound diagnosis is correct (100% tier/model collinearity, n=1 at hard/opus). But it is unresolved against the pacing recommendations that dominate the same report: an A/B over 4 hard-tier slices consumes roughly 4 x 3.5-4.3pp = 14-17% of a weekly plan allowance that is already exhausted most weeks, and R-04/R3 would refuse to launch the arms once the pace line is crossed. As written the experiment will be starved by the loop's own new governor.
reviews.correction: Give the A/B an explicit credit reservation — e.g. the pacing gate carves out N percentage points per plan week for measurement work and treats it as first-call spend rather than residual headroom — and state that reservation as a number the operator signs off on. Otherwise this recommendation is executable in principle and unexecutable in practice, which is how the identical README-promised A/B has already sat unrun for three weeks.

reviews.reasoning: Deleting the gating_test_audit half of mr-audit is well-evidenced (0 true positives across the entire v3 era) and the KEEP of the orchestration half is correctly scoped. But the report as a whole never reconciles its own gate accounting: this recommendation deletes one gate while R-06/R6 adds a per-PR mutation gate, R-11/R3 adds an ADR-residual CI gate, R-22/R9 adds a nightly perf gate, and R-25/R26 tightens the mutation ratchet. Net gate count rises.
reviews.correction: The final report must state the net effect on credits per merged slice, not just per gate. A changed-lines mutation gate that finds survivors converts directly into in-slice rework turns, and rework turns are billed at the RC-5/RC-8 cache-read multiplier (~150k tokens re-read per turn). That is very likely the right trade against the PRIMARY axis, but it is a trade and the report currently presents the deletions and the additions in separate sections as if both were savings. Quantify it with the R-21 plan_util_delta_pp field before and after, and say plainly: this raises credits per slice and buys quality with them.

reviews.reasoning: Confirmed empirically and more urgent than stated. I checked the flag on disk: `.native-supervisor-disabled` EXISTS right now — 0 bytes, mtime Aug 15 17:58 — so as of this postmortem the loop is disabled with literally no recorded reason, actor, or expected-resume, exactly as the recommendation predicts. The rewrite of /home/mdrewt/.local/bin/mr-supervisor-disable to write structured content is concrete and S-effort.
reviews.correction: Add one line to the action: the reader of the flag (mr-native-tick.sh:124-127) must tolerate a ZERO-BYTE flag file forever, because every historical flag is empty and a parser that assumes JSON would fail closed on exactly the arming events that matter most. Treat empty as {who: unknown, reason: unrecorded}.

reviews.reasoning: Both fixes (re-sum on every done-event; per-attempt log paths) are concrete and correctly target measured leaks. But the recommendation treats the ledger's integrity problem as purely an accounting-logic problem and misses that the file itself is undefended.
reviews.correction: Add a third item: the ledger is EXCLUDED FROM VERSION CONTROL and effectively unbacked-up. .gitignore:37 is `memory/projects/*-usage-ledger.jsonl`, `git ls-files --error-unmatch memory/projects/monster-realm-usage-ledger.jsonl` errors with 'did not match any file(s) known to git', and the only snapshots on disk are monster-realm-usage-ledger.jsonl.bak.20260724T170021Z and .bak.20260724T223032Z — both from 2026-07-24/25. So roughly three weeks and ~440 rows of the SSOT exist in exactly one untracked, unbacked-up file, on a machine where every build session runs with --dangerously-skip-permissions and --add-dir on the harness root. Fixing the arithmetic while leaving the artifact undefended is the smaller half of the job. See OMISSION-1.

reviews.reasoning: Material finding no lane examined: the durability of the single cost source. Every cost claim in all three themes traces to this one file, and the file is neither versioned nor backed up.
reviews.correction: MEASURED. The SSOT run ledger is gitignored and unbacked-up, making total loss of the loop's only cost record a live, irrecoverable risk. Evidence: (1) /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/.gitignore:37 reads `memory/projects/*-usage-ledger.jsonl`, and `git check-ignore -v` confirms that line matches monster-realm-usage-ledger.jsonl; (2) `git ls-files --error-unmatch memory/projects/monster-realm-usage-ledger.jsonl` returns "did not match any file(s) known to git" — it has never been committed; (3) the only backups in $MEM are monster-realm-usage-ledger.jsonl.bak.20260724T170021Z (272,981 B) and .bak.20260724T223032Z (275,158 B), both 2026-07-24/25, against a live file of 505,729 B at Aug 15 10:04 — i.e. ~230 KB / ~three weeks of history exists in one copy; (4) mr-record:108 appends with a plain `with open(LEDGER,"a")` and no flock; (5) every build session is launched with `--dangerously-skip-permissions --add-dir "$HARNESS"` (mr-launch.sh:85), so any slice session has unguarded write access to it. By contrast the handoff and mr-state.json ARE tracked (though currently carrying 86 and 10 uncommitted added lines respectively). Fix is trivial and belongs with R-23: either un-ignore the ledger and commit it on each tick alongside mr-state.json, or add a rotating snapshot to the existing tick reconcile path. Cost of not fixing: every measurement in this postmortem becomes unreproducible and the loop loses its only spend history.

reviews.reasoning: Two lanes noted the two handoff files differ 240x in size; nobody checked whether their CONTENT diverges. It does, and recent supervisor reasoning is being written to a path nothing reads.
reviews.correction: MEASURED. The two monster-realm-handoff.md files are not a duplicate and a stub — they are a split brain, and the wrong-path file holds tick history that is invisible to the loop. /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/memory/monster-realm-handoff.md (UNTRACKED, 1,781 B, mtime Aug 15 07:02) contains exactly two entries: '## 2026-08-14T15:59Z — native tick: delegated 14r-e CI-wait' and '## 2026-08-15T11:02Z — native tick: launched 13r-h'. Grepping the canonical /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness/memory/projects/monster-realm-handoff.md (428,676 B, tracked) for '2026-08-14T15:59Z', '2026-08-15T11:02Z', 'delegated 14r-e CI-wait' and '13r-h solo (HARD tier' returns 0 for all four; its three newest headings are 2026-08-15T~09:00Z, 13:22:01Z and 14:03:40Z, so the 11:02Z tick is missing from the middle of an append-only file. Consequence: mr-situation:137 tails ONLY `{MEM}/monster-realm-handoff.md` for its recent_blockers extraction, and mr-supervisor-prompt-native.md:70 names the file with no path ('append-only prose history. Append your entry; read the newest'), so a tick whose cwd or path resolution differs writes where no subsequent tick, and no situation bundle, will ever read. Two ticks' worth of launch reasoning — including the 13r-h launch decision and the 14r-e CI-wait delegation — are effectively lost to the loop. This also means the 'append-only prose history' invariant is already violated. Fix: make the path absolute in both the prompt and mr-record (mr-record:30 writes to HANDOFF), merge the orphan file's two entries into the canonical one, and add a selfcheck assertion that no handoff exists at $HARNESS/memory/. This must be done BEFORE R-15(c)/R-24(3) split the big file, or those two entries are destroyed.

reviews.reasoning: The launcher's actual runtime behaviour was never examined by any lane, and it is the mechanism behind ISO-01 and behind the harness's exposure in OMISSION-1.
reviews.correction: MEASURED. Build sessions are launched INTO THE SHARED MAIN CHECKOUT with all permission gates disabled and the whole harness writable, so worktree isolation cannot be enforced by prose. mr-launch.sh:17-18 sets HARNESS=/home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness and PROJDIR="$HARNESS/projects/monster-realm"; mr-launch.sh:85 then runs `( cd "$PROJDIR" && claude --model "$MODEL" --effort "$EFFORT" --dangerously-skip-permissions -p "$(cat "$B")" --add-dir "$HARNESS" --output-format stream-json --verbose ) </dev/null >>"$L" 2>"$E"`, with the identical flag set on the resume path (:124) and the cost-cap wrap (:139); mr-native-tick.sh:308 uses --dangerously-skip-permissions for the supervisor tick too. Three consequences no lane drew: (1) the session's cwd is the shared checkout every sibling slice also reads, so ISO-01's main-checkout Edit was the path of least resistance, not an aberration — a fix requires changing the launcher's cwd or adding a path allowlist, and must confront the documented reason for the current choice in the inline comment at mr-launch.sh:18 (project-level .claude skill discovery — 31 domain skills, desync-guard, reducer-security-auditor — is only found from inside PROJDIR); (2) --add-dir "$HARNESS" plus skip-permissions gives every slice session unguarded write access to the gitignored ledger, mr-* scripts, the supervisor prompt and mr-state.json, which is the blast radius behind OMISSION-1; (3) mr-launch.sh contains no `trap` and no worktree teardown of its own — the only worktree awareness is a read-only status dump at :31-32 — so cleanup depends entirely on the supervisor tick, which is why the reboot case (OMISSION-4) has no owner.

reviews.reasoning: 'What happens on machine reboot mid-slice' was named in the lens and addressed by no lane. Partial machinery exists; the gap is specific and citable.
reviews.correction: MEASURED, partly reassuring and partly defective. Reboot recovery EXISTS: `crontab -l` shows `@reboot sleep 60 && /bin/bash .../mr-native-tick.sh` alongside the hourly `0 * * * *` entry, and mr-native-tick.sh:114-119 reconciles a run whose session_leader is dead by writing a ledger row `CRASHED(no-done, dead leader $PIDL)`. Three gaps: (1) the liveness test at :115 is `{ [ -n "$PIDL" ] && kill -0 "$PIDL" 2>/dev/null; } && continue` with NO age bound — after a reboot the PID space restarts from low numbers, so a stale low-numbered session_leader can alias a live unrelated process and the tick will treat a dead slice as permanently live, skipping reconciliation forever; contrast the chain-mutex path at :276, which does bound by age ('NOTE stale chain-mutex age=${AGE}s'). (2) On CRASHED there is no step that recovers or even reports uncommitted WIP in the slice's worktree; the only worktree awareness in the launcher is a read-only `git -C "$WT" status --short` dump at mr-launch.sh:31-32. The cost-cap path DOES have the right pattern (mr-launch.sh:138 instructs the session to 'Commit all WIP on the slice branch as wip($S): cost-cap park, push the branch') — a reboot has no equivalent because nothing runs. (3) Current state is clean and worth recording as a baseline: `git worktree list` in projects/monster-realm shows only the main checkout at 67fbff8 [master], and .claude/worktrees/ is empty — so the window's slices did tear down. Residual leak: 13 local branches remain, of which three are stale feature branches (feat/12r-f-ledger-doc-reconciliation, feat/m20a-observability-layer1, feat/uxd3-b-overlay-registry-substrate). Fix: add a max-age bound and a boot-epoch check to the :115 liveness test, and make the CRASHED path attempt the same wip-commit-and-push the cost-cap path already performs.

reviews.reasoning: Every theme discusses the kill switch historically; none checked its current state, which materially raises the priority of R-07/R7/R16/R10.
reviews.correction: MEASURED, as of this review. The kill switch is ARMED RIGHT NOW and carries zero provenance: `ls -la $MEM/.native-supervisor-disabled` returns `-rw-rw-r-- 1 mdrewt mdrewt 0 Aug 15 17:58` — a zero-byte file, no reason, no actor, no expected resume, created hours after the window closed. This is not a historical postmortem item; the loop is off at the moment the report is being written, and no artifact in the tree can say whether that is an operator credit pause (correct, per operator correction D) or a supervisor 'no launchable slice' self-disable (a bug, per DOCT-02/PLAN-02). The report should state this as a live action item, and any flag-reader implementing R-07's structured format must tolerate an empty file (every historical arming is empty) rather than failing closed on exactly the events that matter.

reviews.reasoning: Three separate themes independently recommend the same context-management mechanism, and all three name an API feature the harness's launch path cannot reach. Recorded as its own omission because it invalidates a headline savings claim (~$100/week) shared across themes.
reviews.correction: MEASURED. The context-editing recommendations (theme-1 R-16, theme-2 R4 item 1, theme-3 R24 item 1) are unimplementable as written, and one of them carries a dollar figure the report leans on. All build sessions are started by the Claude CLI, not the Anthropic API: mr-launch.sh:85/:124/:139 all invoke `claude --model ... --effort ... --dangerously-skip-permissions [-p|--resume] ... --add-dir ... --output-format stream-json --verbose`. `clear_thinking_20251015` and the `context-management-2025-06-27` beta are API request-body features; no flag in that invocation sets them and none of the three recommendations names one. The GATE-03 measurement behind them is sound (zero isCompactSummary/compact_boundary events across 230 transcripts, contexts to 611K) — the diagnosis is right and the remedy is unexecutable. Executable alternative inside the existing surface: cap turns per build session and checkpoint/relaunch, reusing machinery mr-launch.sh already has — the --resume path at :124 and the cost-cap wrap prompt at :138-140, which already instructs a session to commit WIP on the slice branch, push, and write a handoff before stopping. That converts an unbounded single context into bounded segments and is an S/M change to the launcher rather than a rewrite. Until one of these is chosen, the ~$100/week thinking-clear saving should be labelled CONTINGENT, not banked.

reviews.reasoning: MCP server usage was named in the lens and is examined by no lane beyond one explicitly-inferred sentence, despite being both a preamble-cost hypothesis and a supply-chain surface.
reviews.correction: OBSERVED + INFERRED. The MCP layer is unexamined in three respects. (1) COST: SINK-02 attributes part of the 44,288-token parent preamble to 'unused MCP servers (Postman, Google Drive, Indeed, Audible, ZipRecruiter etc. are all loaded but never called in any build session)' and its own gaps section concedes this is INFERRED because transcripts store messages, not system prompts. It is directly measurable — launch one throwaway headless session with the current config and one with a trimmed MCP scope and diff turn-1 context — and nobody ran it, so the size of R-15/R24's 'obvious first cut' is unknown. (2) SUPPLY CHAIN: those servers' instruction blocks are third-party text injected into the system prompt of sessions that run with --dangerously-skip-permissions and --add-dir on the harness root (mr-launch.sh:85). No lane assessed that. (3) TOOL ROUTING: NAV-01's finding that the orchestrator makes 0 codegraph calls while its subagents make 47 is compatible with a per-layer MCP availability difference, which nobody checked; if the parent's MCP scope differs from the subagents', the fix is a config change, not the brief-line instruction R24(2) proposes. Verify which before shipping that line — it is still worth shipping either way, but the diagnosis may be wrong.

reviews.reasoning: CodeGraph/codebase-memory index freshness was named in the lens. It is discussed by the lanes only as the source of false probe trips; its actual state — and a duplicate-daemon condition — was never checked.
reviews.correction: MEASURED. Two distinct CodeGraph installations are running simultaneously against this workspace, and the harness's own index appears stale. `pgrep -af codegraph` shows (a) a globally-installed @colbymchenry/codegraph under asdf node 24.13.1 serving --mcp behind a Hermes mcp_stdio_watchdog (pids 1600788/1600793/1600801, plus a watchdog child that SIGKILLs the parent after 60s of unresponsiveness), and (b) a separate /home/mdrewt/.codegraph/versions/v1.5.0 binary serving `--mcp --path /home/mdrewt/projects/ai-apps/claude-harness` (pid 2954072). Index state: projects/monster-realm/.codegraph/codegraph.db is 184,332,288 B with mtime Aug 15 08:58 (fresh, and note its size relative to the repo); the harness's own .codegraph/codegraph.db is 1,593,344 B with mtime Jul 31 14:37 — 15 days old — while its daemon.pid, daemon.sock, codegraph.db-wal and daemon.log all carry mtime Aug 15 16:19, i.e. a live daemon writing logs against a database whose content has not changed in over two weeks. Two consequences: (1) any agent routed to codegraph for HARNESS code (the mr-* scripts this postmortem is about) may be reading a Jul-31 view — which matters because R-18/R-17/R-24 all propose harness-code changes; (2) this continuous daemon.log/db-wal churn is the direct cause of the 90% of probe false-positives SCHED-04/PIA-11 measured, so R-19/R9/R13's exclusion fix is correct but treats a symptom of two daemons that should be one. Verify the harness index is current before trusting any codegraph answer about mr-* code, and reconcile the duplicate installs.

reviews.reasoning: The lens asks for the tradeoffs the final report must resolve rather than paper over. Three are structural across themes and none is resolved anywhere in the material.
reviews.correction: UNRESOLVED CROSS-THEME TRADEOFFS the final report must decide explicitly. (1) PACING vs QUEUE-FILLING: R-04/R3 refuse new launches above the pace line; R-09 forbids standing down while the ready-set is non-empty; R-14/R14 launch elaboration slices when runway drops. In the reviewed week all three conditions held at once. Precedence must be stated — pacing wins, and 'work available, credits exhausted' needs its own logged state distinct from both 'nothing launchable' (bug) and 'operator paused' (correct). Theme-3's R14 guards this with 'AND the plan band is NORMAL'; theme-1's R-09 and R-14 do not. (2) CREDITS vs LENS DEPTH: R3 band (b) demotes hard-tier slices to routine under credit pressure, which thins the review battery on exactly the surfaces (schema/reducer/netcode/security) where the loop's own evidence says rework originates — and a demoted slice that produces a residual costs two slices' credits for one slice of capability, a net loss under the value-per-credit objective. Deferring is free (idle hours cost nothing); demoting is not. Resolve as: reduce N, never reduce tier. (3) NET GATE COUNT vs CREDITS-PER-SLICE: the report deletes one gate (R-12) and adds four (mutation-in-diff, ADR-residual CI, perf nightly, ratchet tightening) in separate sections, presenting both directions as savings. Changed-lines mutation survivors convert into in-slice rework turns billed at the ~150k-tokens-re-read-per-turn multiplier, so this raises credits per merged slice. That is probably the correct trade against the PRIMARY axis, but it must be stated as a trade, measured with the R-21 plan_util_delta_pp field before and after, and sequenced — R-21 (instrumentation) must land at least one cycle before R-06/R-22, which is the explicit lesson RC-7 draws from the v3 cutover and which theme-3's R21 states and theme-1's ordering does not.

reviews.id: QUAL-03 (mutation ratchet 'remediated by RAISING the cap')
reviews.reasoning: The causal claim — that the remediation LOOSENED the gate and that quality got worse — is refuted by the ADR's own measurement table, which I read directly. docs/adr/0183:40-46: baseline commit 9ef0b03 re-run locally = 513 mutants / 299 missed = 58.3% survival; slice head and hosted master = 753 mutants / 324 missed = 43.0% survival. The mutant population grew 47% (real crate growth, proven by re-running the baseline commit and reproducing 299/513 exactly), while the survival RATE fell 15 points. An absolute survivor cap that rises while the survival rate falls is not a loosened ratchet; it is a stale-baseline artifact of using an absolute count as the ratchet unit. The ADR classifies it exactly that way (line 24: 'ADR-0118's class (c) — stale ratchet baseline, not weak tests'), names 11 killable survivors, and commits a successor ratchet to ≤313 (line 9). Presenting '43% of mutants survive' as a new degradation, when the prior state was 58%, inverts the direction of the only semantic quality trend in the corpus.
reviews.correction: Narrow claim that survives: (a) the ratchet UNIT is wrong — an absolute survivor cap must be re-baselined on every crate growth, which is indistinguishable from loosening and produced three episodes of this class; (b) 282 of 324 survivors (87%) remain untriaged, so the population is unexamined; (c) the failure-visibility root cause was documented rather than fixed. Claims (a)-(c) are real. The claim 'the remediation loosened the gate / 43% survival is evidence of decline' is false — survival improved from 58.3% to 43.0%. The right fix is per-module or per-KLOC-normalised ratchets, which theme-3 R26(2) already proposes.
reviews.severity_adjustment: MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE (the ratchet-unit defect and untriaged-survivor backlog are real; the quality-decline framing is not)

reviews.id: QUAL-02 ('source-scan tests are the root cause of the 43% mutation-survivor rate')
reviews.reasoning: The measurement (30-42% of server tests are regex-over-source-text) is solid and is a genuine PRIMARY-axis finding. The causal link to the survivor rate is asserted with no evidence and is contradicted by the ADR the same postmortem cites: ADR-0183 classifies the survivor delta as crate growth / stale baseline explicitly 'not weak tests' (line 24), and of the 41 newly-classified survivors, 32 were legitimate-shell (ctx-taking reducer bodies that no unit test can reach) and only 9 weak-test. The survivor population is dominated by unreachable shells, not by text-scanning tests failing to kill reachable mutants. No one has computed survivor-density in modules with high include_str! share versus low.
reviews.correction: Salvageable claim: source-text-scanning tests pin text shape rather than behaviour, so they under-protect correctness and actively penalise refactoring — which is a direct hit on the operator's PRIMARY axis (changeability) on its own terms, without any mutation-rate argument. Drop the 'root cause of 43% survival' attribution; it is unmeasured and the repo's own triage points the other way.

reviews.id: T3-R6 (replace mr-audit with `cargo mutants --in-diff` as a zero-tolerance merge blocker)
reviews.reasoning: Three independent defects in the argument. (1) IT CANNOT SEE THE DEFECT CLASS USED TO JUSTIFY IT. The headline indictment of mr-audit is that m20b merged CLEAN and shipped an observability stack that crash-looped four of eight containers — four docker/config defects (tempo CLI flag, alloy uid/cap, caddy file-capability, grafana interval). A Rust diff-mutation gate is equally blind to every one of them. The escaped-defect evidence argues for a container boot-smoke test, not for mutation testing. (2) ZERO TOLERANCE IS UNSOUND. cargo-mutants cannot identify equivalent mutants; a zero-survivor blocker on changed lines forces the author to either write assertions that pin implementation detail (the exact pathology QUAL-02 condemns) or add `#[mutants::skip]` to production source — and theme-3 R7(3) simultaneously proposes widening the suppression scan to flag exactly that. The two recommendations manufacture and then flag the same suppression. (3) 'CHEAP BY CONSTRUCTION' IS UNMEASURED. ADR-0183 records 753 mutants in 26 min on a local 32-core box and the hosted nightly averaging ~155 min for the same catalogue — roughly 12s/mutant on ubuntu-latest. A diff touching twenty functions is plausibly 15-25 minutes of added PR CI per attempt, before rebuild overhead, on a loop that already reruns CI 7 times a week.
reviews.correction: Salvageable and genuinely valuable: run `cargo mutants --in-diff` as an ADVISORY PR check that lists named survivors on changed lines and records the count into the ledger (theme-3 R21 already wants the field). Require triage of each survivor into legitimate-shell vs weak-test in the PR body — a judgment the reviewer/red-team roles already do well — rather than a mechanical zero-survivor block. Do not adopt it as the replacement for the escaped-config-defect class; that needs a boot smoke test.
reviews.severity_adjustment: Effort L is right, but sequence it behind an advisory cycle; do NOT ship R7 (defang mr-audit) on the assumption R6 already covers the same slices, because it does not cover the non-Rust surface at all.

reviews.id: T1-RC-4 / T3-RC-2 ('gates cannot fail correctly; the mutation ratchet was fixed by loosening it')
reviews.reasoning: The root cause is largely well established — a 0-precision lexical audit, seven measurably blind security evals, and no perf gate are all real and independently documented. But it inherits QUAL-03's inverted mutation claim as one of its four pillars, and it inherits the m20b crash-loop as evidence that 'gates cannot fail correctly' when in fact no gate in the system was ever scoped to container boot. Those are scope gaps, not gates that fail incorrectly, and they call for different remedies (add a missing gate vs fix a broken one).
reviews.correction: Restate as two distinct causes rather than one: (a) EXISTING gates score lexical shape instead of behaviour (mr-audit, 0/11 precision; the seven blind *-security evals, two proven to swallow the needle) — fix or delete; (b) WHOLE SURFACES have no gate at all (container boot, reducer latency, subscription payload, frame time) — the m20b escape and PERF-01 belong here. Conflating them produced R6, which is a fix for (a) proposed as a fix for (b).

reviews.reasoning: The direction is right and the concrete fix list is the best part of it — strip comment spans, anchor the skip pattern to test-framework call sites, ignore import reflow, and above all drop the test-path pathspec from the SUPPRESSION pass so `#[allow]`/`@ts-ignore`/`nosemgrep` added to production source stops being invisible (GATE-02). Two reasoning weaknesses to note rather than refute. First, '0 true positives ⇒ no yield' ignores base rate: zero survivors could mean nobody weakened a test, and the gate's deterrent effect on a system where the author knows a diff read follows is unmeasured. Second, 'a 0%-precision gate trains its reader to rubber-stamp' is presented across three lanes as a finding; the doctrine lane itself flags it as an inference from the precision rate with no measurement of adjudication quality. It is plausible and I would act on it, but it should not be cited as measured.
reviews.correction: Keep the fix; drop the unconditional hard-tier FLAG (that alone accounts for ≥2 of the 11 and is not a detection); widen the suppression pass to the whole diff. Label the rubber-stamp mechanism INFERRED. Do not delete before the replacement behavioural signal is actually green, and note that the replacement proposed (T3-R6) does not cover the TypeScript half at all.

reviews.id: PLAN-01 / SCHED-01 / PIA-02 idle-capacity quantifications ('98.1 idle hours ≈ 29 slices ≈ $2,800 forgone'; '79.4% duty cycle'; '133h of idle capacity per week')
reviews.reasoning: These are directly contrary to operator correction A, which the same document acknowledges elsewhere: the binding constraint is the weekly credit allowance, which is exhausted most weeks, and idle hours are free. Extrapolating forgone slices from idle wall-clock silently assumes credits were available to build them. They were not: the plan week in question was at 90% real account utilization at the moment the pause began. Under a fixed weekly allowance, 'the loop could have run 29 more slices in those hours' is arithmetically true and economically empty — those slices had no credits to spend. Worse, the recommendation direction implied (raise duty cycle, raise N_MAX, cut merge→launch latency) would have accelerated exhaustion and pushed spend into purchased overage, which operator objective F names as the only true monetary waste.
reviews.correction: The defensible residue: idle time matters ONLY where it strands already-paid work (the M21b-2 done-event blocked 83.9h behind the kill switch is a real loss because its credits were already spent) or where it forces the loop to spend the NEXT week's credits on stale context. Restate all idle-time findings as stranding findings and delete every 'forgone slices/dollars' extrapolation.
reviews.severity_adjustment: PLAN-01 BROKEN_REPLACE -> MAJOR_ISSUE; SCHED-01 MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE (the missing replenishment trigger is real; the throughput loss attributed to it is not)

reviews.id: SCHED-06 (1-hour cron granularity = 7.4h/week of serialization cost)
reviews.reasoning: Measured correctly, valued wrongly. Under correction A, wall-clock latency between a merge and the next launch consumes no credits and therefore destroys no value; it only shifts when the same credits are spent. The lane's own gap note concedes that at least one of the twelve transitions (163.5 min) was genuine master-CI-red triage rather than scheduler idleness, and that eligibility→launch could not be measured. The only genuine cost named — 'a defect found by master CI waits up to 60 min' — is a responsiveness argument, not a value-per-credit argument, and the loop demonstrably ignored a red nightly for five consecutive days, so 60-minute reaction latency is not the binding problem.
reviews.correction: Reframe as: event-driven merges matter because they harvest already-paid work promptly (stranding avoidance), not because they raise throughput. That reframing supports T3-R16 (make the disabled flag event-exempt) and does not support faster cron or higher fan-out.
reviews.severity_adjustment: MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE

reviews.id: SCHED-11 / PIA-13 (fan-out capped at N=2; the N>=3 protocol is unused dead doctrine)
reviews.reasoning: The observation is fine and the 'dead doctrine' verdict is fair. But the implied remedy — 'raising N to the already-Drew-approved 4 on 08-14 would have compressed the tail' (SCHED-11), and PIA-13's 'using it would have consumed the milestone in one evening instead of triggering an 85h self-disable' — is a throughput argument against a credit constraint. Concurrency does not change credits consumed per slice; it changes the RATE of consumption, which under a weekly allowance means hitting the ceiling sooner. On 2026-08-10 specifically, N=4 would have driven utilization from 87% straight through the ceiling into purchased overage. This is the clearest instance in the corpus of a recommendation that improves a throughput metric while worsening the operator's actual objective.
reviews.correction: Keep the finding that the N>=3 protocol is unexercised prompt weight and should be deleted or exercised. Delete the counterfactual claims that using it would have improved outcomes; at the observed burn rate it would have accelerated allowance exhaustion. Fan-out should be gated by the pacing band, which theme-3 R3 correctly does.
reviews.severity_adjustment: SCHED-11 MINOR_ISSUE -> WORKING_WELL-adjacent (N=2 with mr-disjoint gating to N=1 on structural collisions was the right behaviour); PIA-13 keep MINOR but strip the counterfactual

reviews.id: COST-02 (enforcement counterfactual: '$192.85 of spend prevented, $131.15 on M21b-2 alone')
reviews.reasoning: The label 'spend prevented' is wrong under the corrected objective, and the error is load-bearing because three recommendations quote it. Under a weekly allowance that is exhausted most weeks, killing a run at 125% does not prevent credit consumption — it deletes the partially-completed work and returns the credits to a pool that will be spent on something else that same week. The net effect is destruction of in-flight work plus reallocation of spend, not saving. The lane's own data makes this concrete: two of the four counterfactual kills land at 81.7% and 87.9% of real cap on runs that merged cleanly, i.e. the counterfactual destroys two clean slices to 'save' $41. That directly violates operator policy G1 (stranding a half-done slice is worse than idling), which the same document elsewhere treats as settled.
reviews.correction: Restate as: 'with a calibrated estimator, four runs would have received a hard signal at 125% of cap. Under a cooperative stop-flag that makes the session checkpoint and push, this converts uncontrolled overruns into controlled landings; under a SIGKILL it destroys two clean slices to reclaim $41.' The only defensible enforcement action at the hard rung is the cooperative landing-pattern the brief already implements, never a kill.
reviews.severity_adjustment: Keep MAJOR_ISSUE for 'the governor is 100% advisory and 4 slices blew their cap', but the enforcement counterfactual should be labelled INFERRED and its dollar figure withdrawn.

reviews.reasoning: The mechanism is right and this is the single most important recommendation in the set. Two reasoning defects. (1) Its stated benefit — 'prevents the window's defining event: the 09:05Z launch of M21b-2 ($274.37)' — inherits the 'prevented spend' fallacy: refusing that launch does not save credits under a fully-consumed allowance, it reallocates them, and the genuine benefits are narrower (avoid overage, avoid stranding, spend the last 10% on higher-value work). (2) It has no under-consumption guard. Bands keyed on 'util >= 0.85 → launch nothing new' plus a 10pp pace margin will systematically leave allowance unspent in weeks where burn is uneven — and unused weekly allowance does not roll over, so under-consumption is a value loss exactly symmetric to overage. T3-R3 gets this right with its week-1 check ('utilization at reset lands in 90-100% rather than either hitting the ceiling early or finishing under 70% — both are failures'); T1-R-04 does not carry that check.
reviews.correction: Adopt the T3-R3 formulation over the T1-R-04 formulation: the objective is to LAND the week at 95-100% without touching overage, not to stay below a ceiling. State the benefit as (i) zero overage purchases, (ii) zero stranded slices, (iii) the last decile spent on the highest-severity ready item — not as dollars prevented.

reviews.id: T2 conversion anchor ('$1,799.65 ≈ 90% utilization, so 1% of plan ≈ $20 internal-dollars') and every 'returns N pp of allowance' benefit figure
reviews.reasoning: This anchor is invalid and it silently inflates the headline benefit of at least four recommendations (T3-R11 'halving the leak returns roughly 16% of the weekly allowance'; T3-R24 'a 25-40% reduction... roughly 5-8 additional slices'; T1-R-15 'worth roughly 9 percentage points'). The 90% figure is ACCOUNT-WIDE utilization, which the operator's own correction states includes usage on other machines and unrelated projects that no local ledger can see. Dividing harness-only ledger dollars by account-wide percent assumes the harness is ~100% of account consumption — precisely the assumption the correction block denies. If the harness is, say, 75% of account usage, then eliminating 20% of harness spend reduces utilization by ~13.5pp, not 18pp, and every derived 'extra slices per week' figure is overstated by the same unknown factor. Nothing in the corpus measures the harness's share of account usage, and nothing proposed measures it either.
reviews.correction: All pp-of-allowance benefit figures are UPPER BOUNDS contingent on an unmeasured harness share. The fix is cheap and belongs in T1-R-02/T3-R1: once utilization is persisted, correlate observed pp deltas against ledger dollars over intervals where only the loop ran, to estimate the harness share directly. Until that exists, express benefits in ledger dollars or in slices, and state the conversion as unknown.

reviews.id: T1-RC-1 (mechanism: attributing the 1.39x under-report to fable mispricing and estimator bugs)
reviews.reasoning: The conclusion (the governor is blind and must read utilization) is correct and operator-confirmed. The MECHANISM section is a confound: it lists the unvalidated $2783 limit, the uncalibrated fable price, the 1.75x event double-count and the 5m/1h cache-write bug as the explanation for the 1.39x gap between internal 64.7% and real 90%. But the correction block states the gauge is account-wide and includes usage the ledger structurally cannot see. Scope mismatch alone could account for the entire gap with a perfectly calibrated price model. Treating the gap as evidence of pricing error is correlation dressed as cause, and it is what justifies the effort estimate on the pricing-bug fix.
reviews.correction: Split the claim: (a) the governor is blind to account-wide consumption — MEASURED, causally established, and sufficient on its own to justify reading utilization; (b) the internal price model additionally contains two verified mechanical bugs (per-content-block double count; 1h cache writes at the 5m rate) — MEASURED independently from the event stream, and true regardless of (a). The 1.39x gap is evidence for (a) and is NOT evidence for (b); it cannot be decomposed without measuring the harness's share of account usage.

reviews.id: T3-R4 / COST-03 / COST-10 (fix mr-cost-watch pricing bugs; collapse the 0.637-1.008 spread)
reviews.reasoning: The two bugs are genuinely measured from the event stream and the fix is correct engineering. But the priority is inflated by two arguments that do not hold. First, the effort is justified partly by the utilization gap, which it cannot explain (see above). Second, operator decision G2 demotes the dollar model to an interpolator between utilization samples — and the tick runs hourly, so samples are dense. A 24% median bias in a quantity used only to bridge sub-hour gaps is a second-order error. COST-03's own gap note concedes the deduped reconstruction still explains only ~70% of billed cost, so the residual after fixing both bugs is larger than the bias being fixed.
reviews.correction: Keep the fix — it is cheap and it removes a falsified safety argument (mr-cost-watch:82 claims thresholding on raw 'fires early = safe' while M21c and 13r-b measured ledger/raw > 1.0, i.e. raw UNDERCOUNTS). But rank it below the utilization work, and do not gate enforcement on it: the ~30% unexplained residual means the corrected estimator is still not accurate enough to be a kill trigger, only a landing-pattern trigger.
reviews.severity_adjustment: COST-03/COST-10 MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE once G2 demotes the dollar model to interpolation

reviews.id: T3-R5(b) / T1-R-13 (arm costwatch_enforce=true after the accuracy gate)
reviews.reasoning: Part (a) — fixing the brief's false claim that 'only the 125% hard ceiling is mechanical' — is correct, free, and causally well-argued: the one artifact read by the agent that spends the money asserts a stop that does not exist. Part (b) needs a hard constraint the recommendation only half-states. The README's documented objection is not merely a calibration complaint: 'a kill strands locks and hard-blocks relaunch until a human edits cap_override.' That is operator policy G1 verbatim — stranding is worse than idling. T3-R5 does eventually say to use the cooperative stop-flag rather than SIGKILL, but T1-R-13 and COST-02's counterfactual both still reason in terms of kills that 'prevent' spend.
reviews.correction: Bind it explicitly: the 125% rung MUST fire the cooperative stop-flag path (checkpoint, push, PR, exit clean) that the brief already documents at :36. A SIGKILL at any rung is forbidden by G1 and is not justified by any measurement in the corpus — all four historical HARD trips were on runs that merged EXIT=0.

reviews.id: REWORK-01 / T2-RC2 / T3-RC-3 ('46.6% of lifetime spend bought remediation of its own prior output' as value destroyed)
reviews.reasoning: The measurement is sound; the economic interpretation is not, and it is the single most consequential framing error in the postmortem because three recommendations size their benefit from it. The operator's PRIMARY priority is code quality, testability, debuggability and changeability — content expansion is explicitly NOT a focus. Under that objective function, a slice that unblinds a security eval, fixes an observability stack that cannot boot, or adds dynamic coverage to four trade reducers IS durable capability. Labelling it 'remediation of the loop's own prior output' and contrasting it with 'new capability' imports a feature-velocity objective the operator has explicitly disclaimed. The metric is also directly gameable: the remediation share falls if you relabel work or bundle fixes into forward milestones, with no change to the software. Note the corpus contradicts itself here — QUAL-04 and QUAL-05 rate the per-diff craftsmanship and the proof-of-teeth discipline as exceptional, and 74.9% of merged lines are test/eval by deliberate design, which is remediation-shaped by construction.
reviews.correction: The defensible claim is about LATENCY AND REDISCOVERY, not about remediation share. Measurable waste = (i) mean 13.1-day disclosure→remediation latency, during which the defect compounds and is re-disclosed (two items were disclosed twice); (ii) the cost of rediscovering already-known work via a multi-lens review instead of reading a queue; (iii) genuine duplicates like the 13r-c re-spawn ($14.45 for a 7-line comment edit caused by stale queue state). Those total on the order of $50-150/week, not $643. Retire 'remediation share of spend' as a headline metric entirely.
reviews.severity_adjustment: REWORK-01 MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE as stated; the latency/rediscovery reframing remains MAJOR

reviews.id: T3-R11 / T2-R3 (residual registry: 'halving the leak returns roughly 16% of the weekly allowance')
reviews.reasoning: The benefit arithmetic assumes queueing residuals makes the remediation work disappear. It does not. Converting an ADR bullet into a queue row changes WHEN a fix is built and by WHICH mechanism it is discovered; it does not change whether the fix must be built. The $643 of in-window remediation is the cost of DOING the fixes, and it would still be spent — arguably sooner. The only genuinely eliminated cost is the DISCOVERY mechanism, and that mechanism is already the cheapest thing in the system: the weekly review costs $54-74 and yields 7-8 build-ready slices. So the ceiling on savings is roughly one review cycle's cost plus whatever duplicate rediscovery and latency-compounding you eliminate — not half of $643. Sizing a recommendation at ~16% of the weekly allowance on this basis is the clearest instance of a metric-improving-not-software-improving claim in the set.
reviews.correction: The registry is still worth building, on quality grounds rather than credit grounds: right now seven reducer-security gates are measurably blind, two proven to swallow the scan needle, owned by a slice ID ('14r-c-2') that exists in no spec, PLAN or state file. That is a live PRIMARY-axis exposure with an unbounded latency, and a queue fixes the latency. Size the benefit as 'median disclosure→queued latency 13 days → under 1 day', not as a percentage of allowance.

reviews.id: T3-R11 mechanism (CI gate that reds any ADR containing a defer phrase outside a structured block)
reviews.reasoning: This is process ceremony added to fix a problem caused by process ceremony, and it is gameable in the obvious direction: a phrase denylist ('deferred to', 'a later slice', 'future slice', 'parked to') is defeated by writing 'this is out of scope here' or by omitting the disclosure entirely — which is strictly worse than the current state, where at least the residual is recorded in prose someone can grep. The recommendation acknowledges gaming risk in one clause but the enforcement design does not respond to it. There is also a live precedent for the failure mode: the window's only master-red incident (2h11m, commit 62dce75) was a docs-only ADR commit tripping the existing ADR-digest vocabulary gate.
reviews.correction: Invert the enforcement point. Do not police ADR prose; police the PR. Require every PR whose reviewer/red-team output names work outside `touches:` to emit a structured residual row, and make that assertion part of the reviewer role's remit (it already reads the whole diff and is the cheapest, highest-precision detector in the system at ~$1.71/run). Ship the registry and the situation-bundle surfacing; ship the phrase gate as a warning that files a registry row, never as a red.

reviews.id: T1-R-09 / T3-R13 (mr-ready ready-set; 'forbid the self-disable branch unless the ready-set is empty')
reviews.reasoning: The mechanism is right — `after:` having zero mechanical consumers while priority is re-derived hourly from 390 lines of prose is a genuine defect. But the recommendation directly conflicts with the pacing gate and the conflict is never reconciled. The exemplar used to justify it is the 2026-08-10T05:00:52Z standdown; theme 1's own root-cause section records that the SAME tick read `utilization:0.87, surpassedThreshold:0.75`. Had mr-ready existed and forbidden the standdown, the loop would have launched additional slices at 87% real utilization and driven the week into purchased overage — the exact outcome operator objective F names as the true waste. The postmortem treats that one tick as both a queue-derivation bug (PLAN-02, SCHED-02, DOCT-02, PIA-02) and as a correct-but-under-informed pause, and prescribes opposite remedies for it without noticing.
reviews.correction: Build mr-ready — it makes work selection reproducible and lets scarce credits be aimed at the highest-severity ready item, which is the real value under correction A. But state the gate order explicitly: PACING OUTRANKS READY-SET. 'ready_count > 0' must never compel a launch; it may only forbid the claim 'nothing is launchable' as a REASON. And withdraw the four lanes' shared conclusion that the standdown 'cost' 21-85 hours: at 87-90% utilization the forgone launches were not a loss.

reviews.id: SCHED-02 / DOCT-02 / PIA-02 / PLAN-02 ('the self-disable was on a factually false premise and cost 85/117 hours')
reviews.reasoning: The factual core is correct and well cited: seven decomposed slices with `touches:`/`after:` existed, four with `after: none`, in a spec committed five hours earlier, and all four later built with zero additional spec work. The recall failure is real. What is over-attributed is the consequence. Three of the four lanes convert it into hours and dollars of forgone throughput (117.1h latency on a CRITICAL slice; ~29 slices; ~$2,800), which correction A invalidates. And the ground-truth-correction block already establishes that the dominant 85h span was a deliberate operator credit pause, not this standdown — yet PLAN-02 and PIA-02 still attribute the outage to the queue-derivation error.
reviews.correction: Correct claim: the supervisor's work-selection is a prose recall exercise with no mechanical check, and it demonstrably produced a false 'nothing launchable' while four `after: none` slices sat ready. Consequence to claim: unreproducible work selection, so scarce credits cannot be reliably aimed at the highest-severity item (13r-a was CRITICAL and was not selected even when the loop was running). Consequence to DROP: forgone hours, forgone slices, and forgone dollars.
reviews.severity_adjustment: SCHED-02 BROKEN_REPLACE -> MAJOR_ISSUE; PIA-02 BROKEN_REPLACE -> MAJOR_ISSUE

reviews.reasoning: COST-06 itself is exemplary — it identifies total collinearity, refuses to attribute the 2.18x premium, and notes the counter-signal that fable is CHEAPER per file touched ($4.51 vs $4.99). The RECOMMENDATION built on it is the strongest reward-hacking risk in the entire set, for three compounding reasons. (1) NO VALID QUALITY READOUT EXISTS. The proposed outcome measures are post-merge CI red cycles and attempts. remote_red_fix_cycles sums to zero across 446 rows; master_ci_after reads 'pending' on 9 of 17 populated values; the gating audit has 0% precision; and ATTEMPTS is a spawn counter that reads 3 on a clean EXIT=0 build (RETRY-01). An A/B run on these instruments will produce a clean cost signal and a null quality signal, and the predictable, self-serving conclusion is 'no measurable difference, route everything to the cheaper model.' That is a metric win and a potential software loss. (2) NO POWER. n=4 cannot detect a quality difference in a domain whose defect rate is a handful of escapes per 20 merges. (3) IT DELIBERATELY UNDER-ROUTES HARD WORK. T1-R-18 restricts to hard-tier slices excluding auth/RLS, which helps, but hard tier also covers schema/reducer/netcode/reconcile — the surfaces where the operator's PRIMARY priority lives and where a silent defect is most expensive.
reviews.correction: Do not run the A/B until a quality readout with non-zero variance exists — at minimum diff-mutation survivors on changed lines plus reviewer/red-team blocker counts per slice, both of which theme-3 R21 proposes. Pre-register the decision rule: a cost-only result with a null quality result is INCONCLUSIVE, not a licence to downgrade. Absent that, the honest position is COST-06's own: the premium is unjustified AND unrefuted, and tier routing should be made reproducible (T1-R-17) before it is optimised.

reviews.id: PLAN-07 / T3-R15 (spec authoring ran on sonnet by session inheritance — route it to the hard-tier model)
reviews.reasoning: The observation is measured and interesting; the quality inference is unsupported and the remedy is a credit regression. There is no observed quality deficit in the artifacts produced: the same lane's PLAN-11 reports that the 15 review-residual slices derived from these specs were 15/15 merged, 14/15 at ATTEMPTS=1, with 'zero failures attributable to spec ambiguity'. The argument is purely one of routing consistency — 'the slices run on fable so the spec should too' — which is an aesthetic, not evidence. Under the binding constraint (credits), moving a $482 ceremony to a model priced at a config-declared 1.5x guess raises consumption with no measured benefit. This is the mirror image of the fable A/B: there, a cost cut is proposed with no quality readout; here, a cost increase is proposed with no quality readout. Neither is decidable on current instruments.
reviews.correction: Salvageable: spec authoring should be routed DELIBERATELY rather than inherited from whatever session the operator happened to continue — the defect is the absence of any rule, not the specific model chosen. Add the rule; leave the model at the current tier until a spec-quality signal exists (the obvious candidate already exists and is free: downstream slice attempts, parks, and scope re-derivation, which currently read clean).

reviews.id: T3-R15 ('cut the 38-agent ceremony to 1 planner + 3 designers + 1 judge + 1 red-team')
reviews.reasoning: The equivalence argument is a category error: 'the measured quality differentiator is not agent count: it is that both channels emit the same 25-line-per-slice contract.' Format equivalence is not content equivalence. The two channels also solve different problems — the weekly review DECOMPOSES already-verified findings with the answer effectively known, while the heavy ceremony makes open design decisions on a milestone with no prior art. Comparing their cost-per-slice and concluding the expensive one is over-weighted compares a decomposition to a design. The proposed falsifiable bar makes this explicit and worse: 'a pass produces >=5 slices that mr-ready parses and mr-spawn launches without hand-editing vars.json — that is the only quality bar that matters for a spec.' That bar is satisfied by a well-formatted wrong design, and adopting it would make the loop optimise for parseability over correctness. Note also that this recommendation and PLAN-07's (raise the model) push in opposite directions on the same artifact, with no measurement supporting either.
reviews.correction: If ceremony weight is to be cut, cut it on evidence: measure how many of the 38 agents' outputs are cited or acted on in the resulting spec (the transcripts support this and nobody did it). And replace the falsifiable bar with an outcome bar that already exists — downstream slice attempts, parks, scope re-derivation, and residuals emitted per spec — which are recorded and have non-zero variance.

reviews.id: T3-R14 / T1 (unattended spec elaboration as a launchable slice)
reviews.reasoning: This is the textbook 'automate a human judgment whose failure mode is expensive and silent' case, and the recommendation is unusually honest about it, so I will not refute it outright. The residual problems: (1) The justification metric is invalid — '$3/runway-hour vs $15.6-27.6' prices supply channels in hours of loop runway, and correction A says runway hours are not the objective. (2) The guardrail 'terminal state is a PR, not a merge' is weaker than it looks, because a competent review of a milestone spec costs roughly what writing it costs; the realistic failure is a plausible-looking spec that bakes a wrong decision (M22's erase-vs-anonymize policy, retention windows) which then propagates into eight slices before anyone notices. Failure is expensive and silent by construction. (3) The corpus contains zero instances of unattended elaboration on open design space, which the lane's own gaps section states.
reviews.correction: Restrict scope as the recommendation itself half-does, and make the restriction mechanical rather than advisory: unattended elaboration is permitted ONLY for milestones with an existing PLAN bullet stating the decision (M-postgate-client-coverage, M-postgate-roster-wave-3), i.e. decomposition of already-decided work. Milestones with open design decisions (M22-M25) stay attended. Drop the runway-hour justification and justify it as 'removes a 9.2-hour interactive session for work whose decisions are already made.'

reviews.id: T1-R-15 / T3-R24 (context budget: 'halving average context per turn would roughly halve slice cost')
reviews.reasoning: The cost DECOMPOSITION is the best measurement in the whole corpus (90.9% cache mechanics, 34.7% carried thinking, exact from usage.output_tokens). The LEVER claim is correlation dressed as cause. Context volume is largely a consequence of task shape, not an independent dial: the worst orientation share (m20d at 77% before first edit) is the slice that built a 6,053-line load driver and performed a one-off breaking-point measurement — exploration was the work. The 12%-77% spread is presented as 'the addressable part' with no test that the spread is waste rather than task variance. And the asymmetric risk is unstated: cutting orientation on a slice that genuinely needed it produces rework, which under a credit constraint costs twice.
reviews.correction: Split into the mechanical claims, which are strong and safe, and the behavioural claim, which is not. MECHANICAL (adopt): no compaction is configured anywhere across 230 transcripts and one slice ran to 611K of a 1M window with no backstop; the parent preamble is 44,288 tokens against 11,103 for subagents; MCP servers never called in any build session are loaded; the 428KB handoff is grepped at turn 4. BEHAVIOURAL (do not adopt as a target): 'reach first code edit within N turns'. Frame orientation share as a per-slice diagnostic to be explained, never as a budget to be hit.

reviews.id: T3-R24 week-1 check ('first_repo_edit_turn median drops below 35')
reviews.reasoning: This is a directly reward-hackable target and it is proposed as an acceptance criterion. A session satisfies it by making any trivial early edit — touching a comment, adding a TODO, creating the ADR stub — with zero change to how much context it later consumes or how good the output is. The metric moves, the software does not. It is also perverse against the operator's PRIMARY axis: the plan-then-review-then-code gauntlet that QUAL-01 identifies as the best-spending part of the loop is precisely what pushes the first code edit later, so optimising this metric applies pressure against the one mechanism that demonstrably finds merge-blockers before code exists.
reviews.correction: Replace with a non-gameable outcome measure from the same recommendation set: plan_util_delta_pp per merged slice (T3-R21), which is the actual currency and cannot be improved by cosmetic edits. Keep first_repo_edit_turn as a descriptive statistic in the weekly report only.

reviews.id: EFF-01 ('24,125 prompt tokens per line added; a single number for the operator to move')
reviews.reasoning: Offered explicitly as 'a single number to move' while conceding the denominator is crude. As a target it is anti-quality in a specific, predictable way: it improves whenever the loop emits MORE lines for the same tokens. The corpus already shows what that looks like — a single 6,053-line generated test driver, a 10,750-line source-scanning wiring test, 93,641 lines of eval code — and QUAL-06 independently observes there is no simplification pressure anywhere in the loop and 173 total production-source deletions in the window. Adopting a tokens-per-line-added KPI would add pressure in exactly the wrong direction, and the corpus's own better instinct (QUAL-06: '$115/kline of production code is high enough that any slice producing large prod diffs cheaply should be treated as suspect rather than efficient') is the opposite of a line-maximising target.
reviews.correction: Withdraw as a KPI; keep as a trend statistic with its denominator caveat attached. The credit-side headline should be pp-of-weekly-plan per merged slice (T3-R21), and the quality-side headline should be defects escaping to master per merged slice — neither improves by writing more lines.

reviews.id: COST-12 ('the economics reward breadth and punish depth, which is the correct direction')
reviews.reasoning: This is a post-hoc rationalisation of a denominator artifact given a WORKING_WELL verdict. $/kline mechanically penalises deep behavioural work and rewards wide shallow diffs — that is arithmetic, not an economic incentive the system created, and it says nothing about whether the loop is allocating effort well. The lane then reads the artifact as evidence of correct incentives ('the outlier-expensive slices are exactly the ones editing netcode/prediction/auth behaviour — where careful, iterative, expensive work is what you want'), which is unfalsifiable: on this reasoning any cost distribution over any surface would confirm the incentives.
reviews.correction: The genuinely useful content is the composition split (74.9% test/eval, 19.0% prod, and 6,053 of the prod lines being one test tool) and the inversion at the end — cheap large production diffs are suspect. Keep those; drop the WORKING_WELL verdict on the $/kline gradient.
reviews.severity_adjustment: WORKING_WELL -> MINOR_ISSUE (observation retained, incentive interpretation withdrawn)

reviews.id: NAV-01 / T3-R24(2) (orchestrator uses 791 Bash grep/sed/cat/ls calls and 0 codegraph calls)
reviews.reasoning: The doctrine violation is real and orchestrator-specific, which is a genuinely interesting asymmetry (subagents comply with 47 codegraph calls). The COST claim is weaker than presented. The '~$47/week' figure is the carry of ALL Bash tool results (69.7M tokens), of which grep/sed/cat/ls is estimated at ~64% by characters — but a supervisor-of-builds necessarily runs git, cargo, just, gh and test commands, and those results are not substitutable by a code-intelligence tool. Nor is it established that codegraph_explore output is smaller: it returns verbatim line-numbered source for the relevant symbols plus blast radius, which for a broad query can exceed a targeted grep. The savings are asserted, not measured.
reviews.correction: Adopt the one-line brief change — it is nearly free and it aligns the orchestrator with the operator's own global doctrine and with its own subagents' behaviour. Justify it on navigation accuracy (codegraph follows dynamic-dispatch hops grep cannot) rather than on token savings, and measure the delta rather than predicting it.

reviews.id: CONC-01 / ORCH-01 / T3-RC-9 + T1-R-10 / T3-R7 / T3-R10 (fan-out disjointness computed on declared touches the brief silently expands)
reviews.reasoning: This is the strongest causally-established finding in the corpus and I can find no confound. Two artifacts define 'this slice's file set' for different consumers, they are never reconciled, and the consequence is mechanically predicted rather than merely correlated: clause (b) of the companion grant is identical for every slice, so any two concurrent slices are GUARANTEED to collide on ARCHITECTURE.md / CHANGELOG.md / docs/adr/DIGEST.md — and 14r-b's conflict set was exactly that. Clause (a) explains 14r-c/14r-e via main.wiring.test.ts. The fix (expand the effective set from a single shared JSON constant read by both mr-disjoint and the brief renderer) directly addresses the stated mechanism, is cheap, and has no quality downside. The one honest caveat, which T3-R10 states: it will return SERIAL-REQUIRED far more often. Under correction A that costs nothing, since serialisation does not change credits consumed.
reviews.correction: No correction. Add one regression test the recommendation implies but does not state: pin the 14r-c/14r-e input as a fixture that must now return SERIAL-REQUIRED, so the two definitions cannot silently drift apart again.

reviews.id: ISO-01 (14r-c wrote to the shared main checkout while a sibling was live)
reviews.reasoning: Real and worth fixing mechanically. But the severity is over-stated relative to what was measured: the edit and its revert were 7 seconds apart, no damage occurred, and the lane itself notes the brief's prohibition is worded for git commands rather than file writes — so this is arguably not even a rule violation as written. The impact paragraph reaches for 'a transient corruption of the shared checkout during a parallel fan-out is exactly the kind of fault that is near-impossible to diagnose after the fact', which is a hypothetical, not the observed event.
reviews.correction: Keep the recommendation (a path allowlist on Edit/Write is cheap and makes the invariant mechanical rather than prose). Restate the finding as 'the worktree-isolation invariant is unenforced, demonstrated by a harmless 7-second violation' rather than as a near-miss corruption.
reviews.severity_adjustment: MAJOR_ISSUE -> MINOR_ISSUE

reviews.id: CI-01 ('four of the five red nights fell inside the supervisor self-disable, so the only semantic quality gate was failing while the loop was asleep')
reviews.reasoning: This juxtaposition implies the outage caused the missed detection. It did not, and ADR-0183 settles it: 'Nightly has no notification wiring (no webhook, Slack, or issue-creating step anywhere in .github/workflows/nightly.yml)' and 'a documented failure policy existed for smoke-republish only.' An awake loop had no path by which a red nightly would reach it — mr-ci-watch polls PR CI, not nightly. The first red night (2026-08-09) was in fact inside a fully awake period and was equally unnoticed, which is the controlled comparison that refutes the attribution.
reviews.correction: Correct causal statement: nightly red went unnoticed for five nights because nothing converts a nightly failure into an event the loop can see. The overlap with the pause is coincidental and, per the 08-09 miss, not load-bearing. This makes T3-R26(1) — convert a red nightly into a pending-event — the actual fix, and it should not be sequenced behind any scheduler or kill-switch change.

reviews.id: T3-R26 (nightly notification wiring + downward-only per-module mutation caps)
reviews.reasoning: Both halves are well-targeted. R26(1) is the true fix for CI-01 and is confirmed by ADR-0183's own D5 gap. R26(2) is the correct response to QUAL-03's real defect — the ratchet UNIT, not the direction — and 'forbid raising any cap in the same slice that discovers the survivors' is a genuinely good structural rule that removes the conflict of interest. One caution: 'per-module caps that can only ratchet DOWN' will red master on legitimate crate growth (the 513→753 growth was real and verified), so a downward-only absolute cap reproduces the stale-baseline problem it is meant to solve.
reviews.correction: Ratchet on survival RATE per module (missed / viable-mutants), not on absolute counts, and allow the denominator to grow. That is the unit that would have shown the 58.3%→43.0% improvement as green instead of firing five consecutive red nights on real growth.

reviews.id: PERF-01 / T3-R25 / T1-R-22(3) (performance has effectively no gate; wire m20d's load driver to a baseline)
reviews.reasoning: The finding is the best PRIMARY-axis gap in the corpus and is fully supported: seven nanosecond-scale pure-function benches with ~20x headroom, nothing measuring reducer latency, subscription payload, or frame time, and a 6,053-line load driver built and connected to nothing. The recommendation is directionally right but has an unaddressed causal problem: it proposes adding a NOISY nightly gate to a system with a demonstrated five-night reflex of ignoring nightly red, and it proposes replacing the 20x ceilings with tight baseline ratchets on benches whose measurements on shared CI hardware will flake. A flaky perf gate on a loop that pattern-matches red CI to 'unrelated flake' (FLAKE-01: wallet-balance.spec.ts diagnosed four times, never fixed) will be trained into the noise within two weeks.
reviews.correction: Sequence it: R26(1) notification first, then the perf job as advisory with recorded baselines and percentile-over-N-runs ratcheting, then blocking. Do NOT tighten the game-core 20x ceilings in the same change — those are cheap order-of-magnitude smoke and are not where the risk is; the risk is the ungated reducer/subscription/frame surface.

reviews.id: T1-R-01 / T1-R-02 / T1-R-03 / T3-R1 / T3-R2 (read, persist, and govern on rate_limit_info.utilization)
reviews.reasoning: Causally the strongest recommendation set here. The signal is verified present in logs the loop already opens, the consumer count is verified zero, the doctrine's own field enumeration verifiably omits it, and the failure it explains (governor NORMAL at 64.7% while real utilization was 90%) is directly observed rather than inferred. Persisting to $MEM before /tmp ages out is correct and is the part most likely to be dropped as 'obvious'. Three caveats the recommendations handle only partially. (1) Being account-wide, it cannot attribute spend to the loop — both themes correctly keep the ledger for attribution, which must not be lost in implementation. (2) It introduces a coupling with a perverse edge: the operator's own interactive work on unrelated projects will throttle the loop, i.e. the loop is starved precisely when he is at the keyboard and could supervise. That is arguably correct behaviour but will read as a regression and should be documented, not discovered. (3) The staleness rule matters more than it looks — T1-R-03's 'expose util_age_min and treat a stale reading as a floor' is right; any implementation that treats a stale LOW reading as headroom reproduces the exact failure being fixed.
reviews.correction: No refutation. Add: use the persisted series to estimate the harness's share of account consumption (correlate pp deltas against ledger dollars over intervals where only the loop ran). That single derived number is what makes every other 'returns N pp of allowance' claim in this postmortem checkable, and nothing currently proposes measuring it.

reviews.id: T1-R-05 / T3-R3(d) (overage tripwire on isUsingOverage / overageInUse, self-clearing)
reviews.reasoning: Correctly targeted at operator objective F, and the self-clearing design is the specific detail that prevents it becoming a second human-only kill switch — a failure mode this corpus documents twice (2026-07-27 at 74h, 2026-08-10 at 83.9h for a blocked done-event). The evidence for the mechanism is a real logged event, not a hypothetical. No confound found.

reviews.id: T1-R-08 / T3-R16 (split the kill switch; make the operator pause event-exempt and the supervisor standdown self-clearing)
reviews.reasoning: This is the recommendation with the cleanest causal argument in the corpus, and unusually it is supported by an existing in-tree control that already implements the correct pattern twenty lines below the broken one (gate -0.5's wake-file lift, 7-day expiry, and cron-only scoping). It also correctly serves operator policy G1 rather than a throughput goal: harvesting a finished, PR-open, locally-green slice during a credit pause costs ~$1.33 of tick time to avoid stranding $274 of already-spent work. reviews.correction: Guard one thing the recommendation leaves open: the event-exempt path must be mechanically incapable of launching (not merely instructed not to), or it will widen over time into a general bypass — which is precisely how MR_FORCE became a bypass that launched a $274 slice into a disabled loop it could not harvest.

reviews.id: T1-R-17 / T3-R18 (mechanical tier derivation from touches globs)
reviews.reasoning: This is automation of a human judgment, which is the pattern I am told to hunt — but here the failure mode is neither silent nor expensive: the derived tier is recorded on every launch, overrides are logged with reasons, and the observed failures were UNDER-tiering security-adjacent work (m20b, 13r-c), which mechanisation fixes rather than causes. Two real weaknesses. First, a glob table will over-tier at the margin, and over-tiering routes more slices to the expensive model — a credit regression under the binding constraint that neither recommendation prices. Second, the criteria include a hard-coded milestone name ('M20/M25 slices'), which will rot exactly the way mr-tier-map.json rotted into covering 0 of 29 in-window slices.
reviews.correction: Adopt, with the override path retained and logged. Add: express criteria as surface predicates only (schema/reducer, netcode/reconcile, security/RLS, resume-after-park, prior-attempt-failed) and drop milestone-name criteria, which are the component guaranteed to go stale. reviews.id: T1-R-16 / T3-R24(1) (enable compaction and clear_thinking on build sessions)
reviews.reasoning: The measurement behind it is the strongest in the cost analysis (carried thinking = 34.7% of parent prompt volume, computed exactly from usage.output_tokens, and zero compaction events across 230 transcripts). One risk neither states: this loop's entire forensic capability — including this postmortem — depends on session transcripts, and the operator's PRIMARY priority explicitly includes debuggability. Context editing affects the replayed prefix, not the on-disk record, but that distinction must be VERIFIED before enabling rather than assumed, because if it also truncates what is persisted it would destroy the only instrument that measured the problem.
reviews.correction: Add an explicit precondition: confirm on one slice that the on-disk transcript retains full thinking blocks after enabling context editing. If it does not, the recommendation trades a measured ~$100/week against the loop's ability to diagnose itself, which is a bad trade under the stated priorities.

Two flags. A cycle in which every change genuinely helped is a legitimate result.
reviews.correction: Drop escaped_defect_backrefs or assign it to the review role that already reads the diff and can name the originating slice at discovery time. Replace R23's REFUTED target with a process check — 'every mr-changes row whose review window has elapsed has a verdict recorded' — which cannot be gamed by manufacturing a refutation.

reviews.reasoning: The measurements are fine (803 warm-ups, 0 triage invocations ever, tag drift across three 21GB variants). The verdict overreaches on two counts the lane itself concedes. reviews.reasoning: Correctly reasoned and, importantly, correctly JUSTIFIED: both recommendations explicitly refuse the token-savings argument ('carrying the whole prompt forever costs ~$83/yr, 0.087% of spend — that argument would be indefensible') and rest instead on signal integrity, which is the honest case. reviews.id: T3-R19 (falsifier tags on every prompt rule + 120-line hard ceiling)
reviews.reasoning: Diagnostically right — the accretion loop demonstrably froze on 2026-08-01 with 21 dated incident parentheticals across seven July dates and zero August, while the window produced the incidents the prompt says nothing about. But the remedy adds process ceremony to fix a problem caused by process ceremony, and the ceremony's own failure mode is already demonstrated three times in this corpus: mr-feedback, mr-retro-request and mr-metrics were all built as disciplines and all decayed to zero usage. A falsifier tag on every rule is a maintenance obligation with the same shape. The recommendation half-anticipates this ('risk is that a falsifier is written vacuously') without a forcing function beyond mr-prompt-audit, which is itself another unwired script of the kind that has gone dormant three times.
reviews.correction: Keep the 120-line ceiling — a hard budget where adding requires deleting is self-enforcing and needs no new tooling. Drop the per-rule falsifier tag as a universal requirement and apply it only to rules added in response to a specific incident (the class that actually accreted: 21 of them). Wire mr-prompt-audit into the existing weekly report (T3-R23) rather than as a standalone monthly slice, since standalone maintenance ceremonies in this system have a 0/3 survival rate.

reviews.id: T1-R-21 / T3-R15-adjacent (add a loop/process lens to the weekly review; cap at one loop slice per cycle)
reviews.reasoning: Sound, and the one-slice-per-cycle cap is the right guard against loop work crowding out delivery. One causal caveat worth stating: the review is described elsewhere as a flat treadmill that manufactures ~7 residuals per cycle regardless of underlying defect rate, and the trigger is a Cowork cron, not a quality signal. Pointing that same mechanism at the loop risks manufacturing ~1 loop residual per cycle by construction, i.e. a self-perpetuating process-improvement backlog. T3-R12's stopping rule (trigger on open_residuals crossing a threshold, declare convergence when new-residuals-per-merged-slice stays below 0.3) is the right structural answer and should be applied to the loop lens too, not only to the game lens.
reviews.correction: Adopt with T3-R12's trigger-and-convergence rule applied to both lenses. Without a stopping rule, a cron-triggered review that must produce findings will produce findings.

reviews.id: T3-R12 (shrink batch review, grow in-slice review, add a convergence stopping rule)
reviews.reasoning: The causal argument is the sharpest in the set and is mechanically rather than statistically established: a finding raised after a slice merges cannot be fixed inside that slice's closed touches window, so 100% of batch findings become queue items by construction — the batch cadence manufactures the backlog it then measures. Growing the in-slice gauntlet (which fixes findings in the same PR at ~$2/run) and adding an explicit convergence criterion is the correct structural response, and the recommendation honestly marks the quality trade-off and proposes the right guard (keep one full-breadth review monthly; track 'defects first found by batch review that no in-slice lens could have seen'; reverse if that stays high).
reviews.correction: None to the argument. One measurement note: the reversal criterion needs a baseline before the change, and the corpus does not currently classify batch findings by whether an in-slice lens could have caught them. Compute that classification retroactively over 13r/14r before shrinking the batch, or the reversal criterion will have nothing to compare against.
